transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-08
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Chris Moreno (MavenLogic Head of ML), Priya Kaur (Platform), David Ng (CTO)
Links referenced: deck: https://redwood.com/decks/maven-poc, bench csv: https://s3.redwood.com/maven/bench-2026-01-08.csv, security pack: https://redwood.com/security/maven-pack

Summary: Quick weekly sync to review last 48h bench results vs their incumbent, triage a couple of latency outliers, align on next steps for routing + dedicated slot sizing. Call leaned more SE-led for the middle 30 minutes.

Topics discussed: baseline comparisons, 95th vs 50th latency, throughput under burst, routing fallback, VPC/private endpoints, SOC2/SSO concerns, cost for dedicated slots, timeline for canary.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alicia: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call — Alicia from Redwood, Samir from engineering.
[00:10] Chris: Hey Alicia, hey Samir. Chris here, Priya and David on my side as well.
[00:18] Alicia: Cool, objective for today is a focused run through of the CSV you all uploaded, the head-to-head against IncumbentVendorX and decide whether we need a dedicated slot to hit your 99th target.
[00:34] Samir: I'll start with the high level. Over the last 48 hours we ran three kinds workloads: short chat prompts (~200 tokens), mid form completions (1k tokens) and long context synth (4k tokens). We instrumented both Redwood hosted variant and the incumbent baseline with identical prompts and cold/warm caches.
[00:55] Priya: quick Q — how are you handling KV cache on the Redwood side — is that persisting across requests in your bench, or are you warming every run?
[01:05] Samir: Good call. For this run we did a hot KV cache warm for 30 minutes then recorded steady state. In a few tests we forced cache misses to mimic cold starts, which is what caused some of those high tail numbers. You can see the traces in the csv under the warm/cold tags.
[01:24] Chris: When you say 'KV' earlier the transcript had 'K V cash' — ha — but yeah thanks for clarifying.
[01:30] Samir: (laughs) the speech to text is rough.
[01:35] Samir: Looking at numbers — median latency for short prompts is about 12ms token-step equivalence, median is ~38ms end-to-end for short single-shot. 95th is 72ms, 99th jumps to 180ms for short. Baseline numbers are median 45ms and 99th around 250ms. So we have a clear median win and a 99th win but there are outliers.
[02:05] David: Is that with streaming on or off? Our prod is streaming heavy.
[02:10] Samir: These are non-streaming end-to-end to keep a clean compare; streaming adds about 8-12% latency overhead depending on token size. We have a streaming run as well in the csv.
[02:25] Alicia: Chris, you sent us the baseline traces for peak windows yesterday — did you notice particular request patterns matching these tails?
[02:33] Chris: Yeah, we saw that their traffic includes large multi-turn follow-ups and a heavier distribution of 3-4k context calls during our 11am-1pm peaks. That aligned with when we saw the 99th blowups in our system.
[02:50] Priya: For throughput, how close were you to saturating a single slot?
[02:56] Samir: Under steady midsized prompts Redwood delivered roughly 380 requests/min per slot before headroom tightened; baseline needed approximately 1.2x the slots to keep the same qps which is in line with their older compilation path. In burst tests Redwood kept latency below your threshold until about 1.6x burst, after which the tail climbs.
[03:18] Alicia: So on unit economics that's promising — fewer slots for the same throughput but some tail risk during heavy multi-turn periods.
[03:26] David: Can you walk through the tail outliers — cause of the 99th 180ms spikes?
[03:31] Samir: Two main categories: occasional KV cache eviction combined with big context (4k) which forces extra pagewalks, and a handful of kernel warmups where the quantized kernel path recompiled briefly under memory pressure. We're tracking both. The eviction pattern looks like a workload-dependent artifact — on a dedicated slot with pinned cache and reserve memory it largely disappears.
[03:55] Chris: Is that something that a Dedicated config would fix? We're trying to weigh hosted plus burst v dedicated.
[04:02] Samir: Dedicated with pinning + increased cache size and reserved memory reduces eviction events dramatically. Also adjusting the autoscale policy so that we pre-warm at 1.2x expected burst helps avoid kernel recompile spikes.
[04:16] Priya: From compliance: are audit logs and KMS integrated in the private plane? We need end-to-end encryption keys under our KMS and audit stream for long term retention.
[04:26] Alicia: Yes — in Private deployment we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and we ship audit logs with S3-compatible lifecycle. We have SOC2 docs in the security pack. I'll include the link.
[04:38] David: Great. Also cost — show me dedicated monthly vs hosted burst pricing with the 12-month commit.
[04:44] Alicia: We'll update the cost sheet. Quick answer: dedicated reduces per-token unit cost by about 18-24% for your workload profile at the commit size you're looking at, plus predictable latency. Hosted burst is cheaper to start but has higher margin during sustained peak.
[05:03] Chris: Any other configuration knobs you tried that materially changed 99th?
[05:08] Samir: Yes — three knobs: 1) KV cache pinning and reserve pool, 2) quantization profile (we toggled 4-bit vs mixed 8/4 which reduced kernel recompile frequency), 3) finer-grained routing to fall back to a slightly smaller model variant when memory pressure spikes. The last one trades a tiny quality delta for stability.
[05:30] Priya: How big is that quality delta on our prompt set?
[05:33] Samir: On the evaluation set you shared, ROUGE-ish metrics dropped ~0.6 points absolute, and human reviewers flagged fewer than 2% of completions as degraded. We can tie that back to specific prompts in the eval harness.
[05:50] David: We want to avoid quality regressions under the customer support flows. If fallback changes even a small percent on a certain customer template, it could matter.
[05:58] Alicia: Understood — that's why we propose a canary routing policy: route 5% of traffic to fallback for 48 hours with automatic rollback if error/quality regressions exceed thresholds you set.
[06:12] Chris: Let's do that but add an alert on template-level quality drop.
[06:15] Priya: Circling back — can you share the specific test harness commands you used so our SREs can repro locally?
[06:21] Samir: Yes I'll paste the jenkins job and the k6 commands into the csv metadata; it's in the s3 link under README.
[06:30] Alicia: Quick recap of raw numbers in the csv (Samir, feel free to correct): short prompts median 38ms Redwood vs 45ms baseline, 99th 180ms vs 250ms. Mid prompts median 120ms vs 160ms, 99th 420ms vs 610ms. Long 4k contexts medians show larger absolute but similar relative wins.
[07:01] Samir: Correct. Also note we toggled streaming for a run and saw about +10% latency but throughput stays similar for small token bursts.
[07:15] Chris: Any red flags in error rates?
[07:18] Samir: Error rates were negligible, 0.02% 5xx on average, mostly during induced cache-miss tests. Baseline had 0.04% in the same window.
[07:28] David: So next practical step for us is a short head-to-head with Triton config to validate kernel behavior under our 4k context load, and then decide on dedicated slot sizing.
[07:37] Alicia: Yep — we'll do that. Samir will run the Triton config simulation and share csv. We'll also send the security pack and updated cost sheet.
[07:44] Priya: When can you do the Triton sim?
[07:47] Samir: I can run it overnight and push results by Monday EOD (Jan 11).
[07:52] Priya: Perfect.
[07:54] Alicia: Any other blockers?
[07:56] Chris: Not from me. We do want a 60 minute deep technical on VPC routing and private control plane next week — ideally with an infra SME.
[08:06] Alicia: I'll schedule that for week of Jan 19 and invite our infra lead.
[08:10] David: Good.
[08:12] Alicia: Alright we'll wrap. Thanks everyone.
[08:15] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: Some names and acronyms were mangled by auto-transcribe (e.g., 'K V cash' for KV cache, 'triton' sometimes capitalized differently). We kept original utterances where possible.

Closing recap (as read out):
- Redwood shows consistent median and tail improvement vs baseline, with throughput advantages per slot.
- Tail spikes attributable to cache eviction + kernel warmups; Dedicated + pre-warm mitigations recommended.
- Action items: SAM to run head-to-head Triton sim, Alicia to send security docs and cost update, customer to share traces and SLA targets.

Referenced artifacts:
